text:
Here is a detailed 50-minute lesson plan for a mixed-attainment Year 9 class, designed to be engaging, rigorous, and accessible. --- ### Lesson Plan: The Long Fuse – Causes of the First World War **Class:** Year 9 History (34 students) **Topic:** The Long-Term Causes of WWI (MAIN) **Time:** 50 minutes **Curriculum Link:** Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world 1901–present: the causes of the First World War. --- #### Lesson Objectives (What you will learn): - **All students will:** Identify the four main long-term causes of WWI (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism). - **Most students will:** Explain how these causes created tension in Europe. - **Some students will:** Evaluate which cause was the most significant trigger. --- #### Resources: - Projector & slides (with images and keywords). - **One A4 sheet per student** (see below – double-sided). - Whiteboards and pens (or scrap paper) for quick checks. - Coloured pencils/pens (if available, but not essential). --- ### Lesson Structure | Time | Activity | Teacher & Student Activity | Purpose & Differentiation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **0-5 mins** | **Starter: The Domino Effect** | **Teacher:** Project an image of a row of dominoes. Ask: *"What happens if I push the first one?"* Take 2-3 answers. Link to the idea of a chain reaction.
**Student Task:** On their mini-whiteboard, write one word they associate with the First World War. Teacher scans answers (e.g., trenches, Germany, guns). | **Hook:** Visual and accessible. Activates prior knowledge. Low-stakes retrieval. | | **5-10 mins** | **Setting the Scene: The Patient & The Diagnosis** | **Teacher:** Introduce the lesson as a "medical investigation." Europe in 1914 was a patient with a fever. We are going to diagnose the causes.
**Slide:** Show a map of Europe in 1914. Point out the major powers (Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Austria-Hungary).
**Key Question:** Write on board: *"Why did a local argument in the Balkans turn into a World War?"*
**Hand out the A4 sheet.** | **Contextualisation:** Makes abstract concepts concrete. The A4 sheet is the central resource for the lesson. | | **10-25 mins** | **Main Activity 1: The "MAIN" Diagnosis (Jigsaw)** | **Teacher:** Explain the acronym **MAIN** (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism).
**Student Task (Pairs):** Using the **top half** of their A4 sheet, students work in pairs. Each pair is assigned **one** of the four causes (e.g., 8-9 pairs per cause). They must read the short text box and complete the "Symptoms" section (bullet points) for their cause.
**Teacher Role:** Circulate. Target support for the 6 students with lower reading ages. Sit them with stronger readers. For these students, pre-highlight the key sentence in each box on their sheet. | **Chunking:** Students only read one small section.
**Peer Support:** Mixed-attainment pairs.
**Active Learning:** They are summarising, not just copying. | | **25-35 mins** | **Main Activity 2: Expert Share & Graphic Organiser** | **Teacher:** Ask for a volunteer from each "cause group" to share their findings. As they do, the teacher projects a blank version of the **bottom half** of the A4 sheet (the spider diagram).
**Student Task:** As each cause is explained, all students fill in the central spider diagram on their sheet, adding a key fact and a symbol/drawing for each cause.
**Teacher:** Emphasise the **interconnection**. E.g., "Alliances were meant to keep peace, but they created two armed camps." Use the domino image again. | **Consolidation:** Transforms individual knowledge into shared understanding.
**Visual Learning:** The spider diagram supports all students, especially visual learners and those with weaker literacy. | | **35-43 mins** | **Main Activity 3: The Spark – The Assassination** | **Teacher:** Project a dramatic image of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife. Tell the story briefly (the failed bomb, the wrong turn, Gavrilo Princip).
**Student Task:** On the back of their sheet (or in books), students answer a "Quick 60-Second Write": *"Explain how the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand was the 'spark' that lit the 'powder keg' of Europe."*
**Sentence Starter (on board):** *"The assassination was the spark because... The powder keg was already full because of... (M)ilitarism, (A)lliances, (I)mperialism, (N)ationalism."* | **Application:** Students apply the MAIN causes to a specific event.
**Scaffolding:** The sentence starter provides structure for weaker writers. The challenge for higher attainers is to write 3-4 sentences without the starter. | | **43-50 mins** | **Plenary: Check for Understanding & Exit Ticket** | **Teacher:** Quick-fire quiz on mini-whiteboards.
1. What does the 'A' in MAIN stand for?
2. Which country did Germany fear being surrounded by? (Russia & France)
3. True or False: Imperialism is about building a large army. (False – it's about building an empire).
**Final Check (The Bell):** Students must not pack up until they have completed the **Exit Ticket** on the bottom of their A4 sheet. They tick one box and complete the sentence. Teacher collects the sheets as students leave. | **Assessment:** The whiteboard quiz is a quick, low-stakes check for the whole class. The exit ticket provides individual data for the teacher to plan the next lesson. | --- ### The Single A4 Sheet (Double-Sided) **Side 1: The "MAIN" Diagnosis Sheet** **(Top Half - Four boxes)** | **M - MILITARISM** | **A - ALLIANCES** | | :--- | :--- | | **What is it?** The build-up of huge armies and navies. Countries wanted to have the biggest and best weapons. Britain and Germany had a naval race. | **What is it?** Treaties between countries to help each other if attacked. Europe was split into two main groups: The Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy). | | **Symptoms (write 2 bullet points):**
-
- | **Symptoms (write 2 bullet points):**
-
- | | **I - IMPERIALISM** | **N - NATIONALISM** | | **What is it?** The competition for colonies (land) in Africa and Asia. Countries like Britain and France had huge empires. Germany wanted one too, causing jealousy and rivalry. | **What is it?** Extreme pride in your country. Some groups, like the Serbs, wanted their own country and hated being ruled by Austria-Hungary. This was very strong in the Balkans. | | **Symptoms (write 2 bullet points):**
-

Students fill in one key fact and draw a small symbol in each box.]* --- **Side 2: The Spark & Exit Ticket** **The Spark: The Assassination in Sarajevo (June 1914)** Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, visited Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. A Serbian nationalist group called the Black Hand wanted to free Bosnia from Austria-Hungary. They tried to kill him with a bomb, but failed. Later that day, the Archduke's driver took a wrong turn. By chance, he stopped right in front of one of the assassins, Gavrilo Princip, who shot and killed the Archduke and his wife. **Quick 60-Second Write:** Explain how this assassination was the "spark" that lit the "powder keg" of Europe. ______________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________ ______________________________________________________________________ --- **Exit Ticket: Before you leave...** **Tick one box:** - [ ] I can name all four causes of WWI. - [ ] I can explain one cause in detail. - [ ] I can explain how the causes are linked. **Complete the sentence:** The most important long-term cause of WWI was ______________________ because ______________________________________________________________________ --- ### Checking Understanding Before the Bell 1. **Mini-Whiteboard Checks (Formative):** The quick-fire quiz at the end (43-45 mins) is the primary live check. It allows you to see instantly who has grasped the core vocabulary and concepts. If a majority get an answer wrong, you can re-teach that point immediately. 2. **Circulation & Questioning (Formative):** During the jigsaw activity (10-25 mins), your targeted questioning of pairs (e.g., "Why was Germany worried about Britain's navy?") allows you to assess depth of understanding, not just recall. 3. **The Exit Ticket (Summative):** This is the final, individual check. It is designed to be quick and non-threatening. The first tick-box tells you about their confidence and recall. The sentence completion tells you about their ability to prioritise and justify, which is a key historical skill. You can sort these into three piles (green/amber/red) as they leave the room to plan the next lesson's differentiation. This ensures you have a concrete measure of learning *before* the bell rings, not just at the end of the unit.
